Take with food to reduce GI upset
Avoid; teratogenic concerns (use only if essential)

summary: Prothionamide is a thioamide second-line antimycobacterial, structurally related to ethionamide, used in regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and in some multidrug regimens for leprosy. Typical dosing is about 15-20 mg/kg/day (commonly 500-750 mg) given with food and often with pyridoxine. It is frequently limited by gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity, hypothyroidism and neuropsychiatric effects. It is not FDA-approved; information derives from WHO, EMA/SmPC and BNF sources.
indications: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (as part of a combination regimen)
Leprosy (as a component of multidrug therapy, second-line)

dosage.d: 15-20 mg/kg/day (usually 500-750 mg) once daily or in divided doses
dosage.n: Always combined with other antitubercular drugs; add pyridoxine

dosage.d: 5-10 mg/kg/day (about 250-375 mg/day) within a multidrug regimen
Give with food, at bedtime, or in divided doses to improve tolerance
dosage.n: Slow build-up of dose may help

admin: Take with or after food to reduce nausea
Co-administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to reduce neuropathy
Build the dose up gradually if intolerance occurs
Always use as part of a multidrug regimen - never as monotherapy
moa: Prothionamide is a prodrug activated by mycobacterial EthA; the active form inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (via the InhA/enoyl-ACP reductase pathway), disrupting cell-wall formation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. leprae. Its action and resistance overlap with ethionamide and partially with isoniazid.

absolute: Severe hepatic impairment / active liver disease

preg: Animal data raise teratogenicity concerns and human data are limited; avoid in pregnancy unless treatment of resistant tuberculosis is essential and no safer alternative exists, under specialist guidance.
lact: Limited data on excretion in breast milk; use with caution and monitor the infant if breastfeeding during therapy.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; dose reduction or extended dosing intervals may be needed in severe impairment, with close monitoring.
hepatic: Hepatotoxic - can cause hepatitis and raised transaminases. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; monitor liver function before and during treatment and stop for significant hepatotoxicity.

major: Other hepatotoxic antitubercular drugs (isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin) - additive hepatotoxicity
Ethionamide - do not combine (same class, additive toxicity)
moderate: Cycloserine - increased CNS toxicity (seizures, psychiatric effects)
minor: Pyridoxine - reduces neuropathy risk (beneficial, give concurrently)
interactions.food: Take with food to improve tolerability.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; risk of psychotic reactions and additive liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise liver enzymes, lower thyroid hormones (raise TSH) and disturb blood glucose.

monitoring: Baseline and periodic liver function tests
Vision and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy
Mental state for depression or psychosis
counsel: Take with food and take your vitamin B6 as prescribed to reduce side effects
Do not drink alcohol while on this medicine
Report yellowing of the eyes/skin, severe tiredness, low mood, numbness/tingling or vision changes
Take exactly as prescribed with your other TB/leprosy medicines - do not stop early
Tell your doctor if you are diabetic or have thyroid problems
pk: Antimycobacterial effect over weeks within a regimen
Plasma peak ~1-3 h after oral dose
Store below 25-30 C in a dry place, protected from light
pearls: Not FDA-approved; used per WHO MDR-TB guidance, EMA/SmPC and BNF
Closely related to ethionamide - shares efficacy and toxicity; do not combine the two
Monitor thyroid function - hypothyroidism is common, especially when combined with PAS
GI intolerance is the main limiting effect; take with food and titrate
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and continue the regular schedule. Do not double the dose. Avoid frequent missed doses to prevent resistance.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe GI symptoms, neurological and psychiatric effects and hepatotoxicity. There is no specific antidote; manage with supportive care and high-dose pyridoxine may help neurotoxicity. Monitor liver function.
